question: Why does my lower back hurt?

say: The world's leading cause of disability.
Most people get it at least once.
And about nine cases in ten can't be pinned on any disease or damage.
Scan people with no back pain: thirty-seven percent of twenty-year-olds show it. At eighty, ninety-six percent.
The authors' verdict: normal ageing. Not disease.
Back pain usually eases within a few weeks.
A review of twenty-nine trials: no better in the long run than other exercise.
The NHS says: stay active, carry on with your day, and don't stay in bed for long.
Not easing after a few weeks, worse at night, or losing weight without trying?
Pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs, lost feeling around your genitals or anus, or changes in peeing or pooing?

screen.show: Trophy plate: No. 1, cause of disability, worldwide
Light box: ten case films, nine stamped NON-SPECIFIC
Scan grids of people with no back pain: 37% at age 20, 96% at age 80; note: 33 studies, 3,110 people; stamp: normal ageing, not disease
Pain out of 100: 52 at the start, 23 at six weeks
73% had it again within a year
Tag: core stability exercise, the dead bug

whofacts: World Health Organization, Low back pain (fact sheet, 19 June 2023): "LBP is the single leading cause of disability worldwide and the condition for which the greatest number of people may benefit from rehabilitation."; "LBP can be experienced at any age, and most people experience LBP at least once in their life."; "Non-specific LBP is the most common presentation of LBP (about 90% of cases)."; "Non-specific means that the experience of pain cannot be confidently accounted for by another diagnosis such as an underlying disease, pathology or tissue damage."
brinjikji2015: Brinjikji W et al. Systematic literature review of imaging features of spinal degeneration in asymptomatic populations. AJNR Am J Neuroradiol 2015;36(4):811 to 816: "Thirty-three articles reporting imaging findings for 3110 asymptomatic individuals met our study inclusion criteria."; Table 2 (model estimates, people with no back pain): disk degeneration 37% at age 20, 96% at age 80; incidental findings "should be considered as normal age-related changes rather than pathologic processes"
nhsback: NHS, Back pain (last reviewed 5 March 2026): "It usually improves within a few weeks but can sometimes last longer or keep coming back."; Do: "stay active and try to continue with your daily activities"; Don't: "do not stay in bed for long periods of time"; See a GP if: "it does not improve after treating it at home for a few weeks", "it does not improve after resting or is worse at night", "you've lost weight without trying to"; Call 999 or go to A&E if: "pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs", "a loss of feeling around your genitals or anus", "changes in your bladder or bowels, such as difficulty peeing, or peeing or pooing yourself"
menezescosta2012: da C Menezes Costa L et al. The prognosis of acute and persistent low-back pain: a meta-analysis. CMAJ 2012;184(11):E613 to E624: 33 cohorts, 11 166 participants; in acute pain cohorts, mean pain out of 100 fell from 52 at baseline to 23 at 6 weeks; "Patients who presented with acute or persistent low-back pain improved markedly in the first six weeks."
acp2017: Qaseem A et al. Noninvasive Treatments for Acute, Subacute, and Chronic Low Back Pain: A Clinical Practice Guideline From the American College of Physicians. Ann Intern Med 2017;166(7):514 to 530: "Given that most patients with acute or subacute low back pain improve over time regardless of treatment"
pengel2003: Pengel LHM et al. Acute low back pain: systematic review of its prognosis. BMJ 2003;327:323: "73% of patients had at least one recurrence within 12 months."; "None the less, pain and disability are typically ongoing, and recurrences are common."
smith2014: Smith BE, Littlewood C, May S. An update of stabilisation exercises for low back pain: a systematic review with meta-analysis. BMC Musculoskelet Disord 2014;15:416: "29 studies were included"; "When compared with alternative forms of exercise, there was no statistical or clinically significant difference."; "There is strong evidence stabilisation exercises are not more effective than any other form of active exercise in the long term."
